questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain the pattern assumption behind containment

options.text: That aid could be justified only by a treaty already in force

options.misconception: ranks economic recovery ahead of every security commitment
options.text: That economic recovery had to come before any commitment of troops

questions.explanation: An oath asks for a promise and punishes a refusal, and a person can give one while holding the views in question, so the newer law attached the penalty to the fact of belonging, which the party's own books documented and could not be disclaimed. The tempting answer drops the evidence requirement, but the statute worked because the records made membership provable, not because proof was unnecessary.
questions.hint: What can a person promise and still believe the opposite of?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Hearings as a source of leverage
questions.learningObjective: analyze how publicity produced losses no official body could impose
questions.stem: A committee's hearings brought in witnesses who named colleagues, and one witness who refused to answer became more famous than most who testified. What made that method powerful?

options.text: Public names created losses that no official inquiry could impose

options.misconception: credits the transcripts rather than the naming
options.text: The transcripts were published in full by the government printer

options.misconception: gives the committee power over broadcast media
options.text: The committee could subpoena witnesses from the television networks

options.misconception: credits television coverage as the mechanism
options.text: The hearings were taped and rebroadcast on the national networks

questions.explanation: Naming a person did something no board could, which was to make ordinary employers and studios decide whether to keep that person, and the fear of that decision spread through workplaces where no committee had ever gone. The tempting answer puts the power in the coverage, but publicity only carried the names; the losses came from other people acting on them.
questions.hint: Who acted on a name once it had been said aloud?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how an unwritten rule multiplied its own reach
questions.stem: A producer who would hire no one named on a private list kept that position for years while denying in public that any list existed, and the number of people affected ran into thousands. How does that pattern work?

options.text: A quiet rule costs less to obey than to challenge, so it spreads

options.misconception: assumes the lists were public documents
options.text: Private lists were published in the newspapers each week

options.misconception: attributes the effect to court orders
options.text: Courts ordered every listed person barred from the trade

options.misconception: misattributes the list to union hiring rules
options.text: Unions required employers to hire only from listed names

questions.explanation: Nobody had to enforce a written rule for it to bind, because a producer could avoid a costly public fight simply by hiring the next person, and that private decision multiplied across thousands of jobs without any agency acting. The tempting answer makes the list public, which is the opposite of its purpose, since a rule that is unrecorded cannot be challenged, only obeyed.
questions.hint: What did it cost to refuse the list quietly?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Domestic sources of the second Red Scare
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the domestic pressures behind a climate of suspicion
questions.stem: In the late 1940s unions were being broken, businesses faced new taxes and foreign competitors, and families had moved quickly from farms to cities. How does that setting explain the intensity of the fear of subversion?

options.text: Uncertain wages and unfamiliar neighbors made any promise look better

options.misconception: claims rural life prevented political rumor
options.text: Farm families had long been immune to rumor and suspicion

options.misconception: treats taxation as reducing political organization
options.text: Taxation reduced the number of groups available to be watched

options.misconception: assumes universal confidence in the economy
options.text: The economy grew so quickly that nobody doubted their place

questions.explanation: Suspicion of this strength needed something to attach to, and workers watching their wages and their neighborhoods change had reason to hope an outside force would explain it, so the hunt for internal enemies answered a domestic anxiety without any espionage having to be discovered. The tempting answer treats the era as uniformly confident, but confidence was what the fear defended against, not what it grew from.
questions.hint: What did an outside enemy offer to people whose world had shifted?

questions.learningObjective: analyze how defense spending creates interests that persist
questions.stem: A former president warned that a military establishment and an arms industry would together grow so large that no president could check them. What mechanism was he describing?

options.text: Contracts, jobs, and plants tied many voters to continued spending

options.misconception: invents a constitutional grant to the military
options.text: Officers had amended the constitution to give themselves a budget

options.misconception: claims the industry chooses legislators
options.text: The industry had begun selecting members of the legislature

options.misconception: reports an absolute share of the budget
options.text: Defense spending exceeded every other federal item combined

questions.explanation: A warning about institutions is a warning about interests, and here the interests were concrete, since a supplier's revenue, an engineer's job, and a town's payroll all had a stake in the next appropriation. The tempting answer turns that web of obligations into a legal power, when nothing in the arrangement gave the military or its suppliers authority; the influence ran through the votes of people whose livelihoods were at stake.
questions.hint: Whose paycheck depended on the next appropriation?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how publicly funded discoveries became civilian goods
questions.stem: Spending on missiles and calculating machines for the armed forces paid for work whose results turned up in ordinary households decades later. What best explains that transfer?

options.text: Public laboratories kept discoveries open and researchers mobile

options.misconception: invents a legal duty to market consumer products
options.text: The military had been assigned by law to market consumer goods

options.misconception: claims the research was sold to private firms
options.text: Companies bought the finished research for a fixed sum

options.misconception: restricts the devices to defense contractors
options.text: Only firms that held defense contracts received the devices

questions.explanation: Public money paid for work whose results stayed available to anyone, and researchers moved freely between laboratories and universities, so a device designed for war reached ordinary households without anyone deciding it should. The tempting answer invents a market assigned by law, when the transfer happened because the research was neither owned by the military nor restricted to firms that sold to it.
questions.hint: Who owned the result of work the government paid for?
